records.sourceFile: The Power of Belief - Investigating the Placebo Effect in Post-Exercise Recovery Strategies for Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Pernigoni M, Alfieri AO, Kniubaitė A, Kamandulis S, Conte D, Lukonaitienė I. The Power of Belief: Investigating the Placebo Effect in Post-Exercise Recovery Strategies for Football Players. Healthcare. 2026;14:4.
paper.abstract: The study asked whether a placebo intervention changes the time course of recovery after a football match. Eighteen youth male players completed two friendly matches in a randomized crossover design, followed by sham vagus nerve stimulation (placebo) or passive rest. Match play caused significant fatigue in jump, sprint, heart rate variability, soreness and perceived fatigue. No significant between-intervention differences were found at any time point, but effect sizes showed moderately lower perceived fatigue and dynamic soreness after the placebo at post-recovery. The authors conclude that placebo stimulation did not affect performance or heart rate variability but may support perceptual recovery.
paper.tldr: In youth soccer players, a sham vagus nerve stimulation device did not change jump, sprint or heart rate variability recovery after a match compared with passive rest. Soreness and fatigue scores looked somewhat better after the sham session, but these differences were not statistically significant.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover design with two friendly 11-a-side matches separated by 72 h. After each match, players sat for 20 min with either an inactive (sham) stimulation device (placebo) or in a quiet room (passive rest). Countermovement jump, 10 and 20 m sprint, Ln-rMSSD, static and dynamic soreness and perceived fatigue were measured pre-match, post-match, post-recovery and at 24 h. Linear mixed models and Friedman and Wilcoxon tests were used, with effect sizes reported.
paper.findings: Match play significantly worsened countermovement jump, 10 m and 20 m sprint and Ln-rMSSD, and increased soreness and perceived fatigue, compared with pre-match. No significant time by intervention interaction was found for countermovement jump (p = 0.850), 10 m (p = 0.171), 20 m (p = 0.402) or Ln-rMSSD (p = 0.370), and no intervention main effect was significant. Effect sizes favored the placebo for dynamic soreness at post-recovery (r = 0.32) and perceived fatigue at post-recovery (r = 0.40) and pre-match (r = 0.34). Analysed sample was 18 players for performance and heart rate variability and 16 for perceptual measures.
paper.limitations: Small single-team sample of youth males. Belief in the placebo was not measured. The placebo was compared with passive rest, not with a real recovery method. Perceived fatigue was already moderately lower in the placebo condition before the match, a baseline imbalance the authors acknowledge. Perceptual analyses include only 16 players, because nonparametric tests could not handle the missing 24 h data, and the study was powered on a single earlier study's effect size.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes' expectations about a recovery tool may matter for how they feel, so staff could consider how recovery options are explained. This study does not show a physical benefit from a sham device, so it should not replace evidence-based recovery or guide training load decisions. Future trials could include a placebo arm and a real recovery arm alongside passive rest, as the authors suggest.
paper.athleteDev: After a match, a sham stimulation device did not improve jump, sprint or heart rate variability recovery in youth players. Soreness and fatigue scores were somewhat lower after the sham session, but not significantly, so they should not be used to set training loads.
paper.rtp: Players were injury-free and the study measured short-term recovery after a friendly match, not return to play after injury, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The Temporal Relationship Between    Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Skorski S, Mujika I, Bosquet L, Meeusen R, Coutts AJ, Meyer T. The Temporal Relationship Between Exercise, Recovery Processes and Changes in Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019.
paper.abstract: A brief review of the time courses of recovery across physiological systems after training and competition, and how they relate to changes in performance. The authors argue that recovery should be tailored to the individual athlete and periodized across the season.
paper.tldr: Different physiological systems recover on different timelines, and those timelines rarely match the return of performance. Recovery strategies should be individualized and periodized, because too much recovery can blunt training adaptation.
paper.methods: Narrative review of studies on recovery time courses in metabolic, neuromuscular, central and cardiocirculatory systems, with examples from team-sport and endurance studies. No search strategy is described. Two schematic figures show hypothetical time courses for carbohydrate resynthesis, inflammation, muscle damage, soreness and voluntary activation.
paper.findings: In team-sport athletes, maximal strength, vertical jump and sprint performance are significantly impaired immediately after exercise, with full recovery taking 12 to more than 72 h. Inflammation markers peak 24 to 48 h after a soccer match and return to baseline by 48 to 120 h, while neuromuscular function returns to baseline between 5 and 96 h. Muscle glycogen can take 2 to 3 days to resynthesize after high-intensity training, and cardiac autonomic control returns to baseline in about 48 h on average. The authors conclude that no single parameter has yet shown a direct, causal link with performance recovery.
paper.limitations: No systematic search is described, and the authors do not state how studies were selected. The authors note that results on the long-term effects of recovery interventions such as cold water immersion are still controversial. The time-course figures are hypothetical and schematic, not measured data.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should plan recovery around the training stimulus, since different systems recover on different timelines, rather than applying one fixed recovery window. Because physiological markers rarely track performance, staff should monitor several measures alongside performance tests. Recovery interventions should be periodized, since too much recovery can blunt adaptation in some training phases.
paper.athleteDev: Use the different recovery timelines to space hard sessions, and track neuromuscular and performance measures across days rather than relying on one marker. Match recovery interventions to the training phase, since the authors note that some studies found regular cold water immersion blunted hypertrophy adaptations during strength training periods.
paper.rtp: The review reports that neuromuscular function after team-sport matches returns to baseline over roughly 5 to 96 h, which can inform expectations for match fatigue. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria after injury, because it addresses training and match fatigue, not injury rehabilitation or clearance.

records.sourceFile: The correlation between sleep quality and performance in football athlete.pdf

paper.citation: Penggalih MHST, Sofro ZM, Oktarini KS, Ningrum RK. The correlation between sleep quality and performance in football athlete. Sleep and Biological Rhythms. 2021.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study of 100 male football athletes examined whether sleep quality, measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, is related to resting heart rate, blood pressure and VO2max measured by bleep test. The authors report significant correlations between sleep quality and all four indicators (p < 0.001), and conclude that sleep quality is related to the performance of football athletes.
paper.tldr: In 100 male youth football academy students, poorer self-reported sleep went with higher resting heart rate and blood pressure and lower VO2max. The design shows association at one point in time, so it supports tracking sleep alongside fitness markers, not a claim that sleep changes performance.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 100 male students aged 13 to 18 at a football academy in Indonesia. Sleep quality was assessed with the PSQI (good if 5 or below), and resting heart rate and blood pressure were measured on waking with a digital sphygmomanometer. VO2max was measured with a bleep test, and Pearson and gamma correlation tests were used.
paper.findings: Eighty-two percent of players had poor sleep quality, and 25% had a resting heart rate of 60 bpm or below. Pearson correlations with PSQI score were 0.384 for resting heart rate (r2 = 0.14), 0.421 for systolic pressure (r2 = 0.17), 0.469 for diastolic pressure (r2 = 0.21) and -0.412 for VO2max (r2 = 0.16), all p < 0.001. Gamma correlations were 0.768 for resting heart rate, 0.773 for systolic pressure, 1.00 for diastolic pressure and 0.68 for VO2max, and the authors describe 18% of players with good sleep as also having good resting heart rate, blood pressure and VO2max scores.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional, so no causal direction can be drawn, and only 18 players had good sleep quality. Sleep apnea, body mass index, diet, lifestyle and training adaptation were not examined, and the study does not measure sport performance. The abstract gives the diastolic coefficient as 4.69, while Table 4 gives 0.469, and the text states that 75% had high resting heart rate where Table 2 labels the same 75% as normal.
paper.practicalImplications: Ask young players to track sleep with a questionnaire such as the PSQI, and read sleep alongside resting heart rate, blood pressure and fitness testing when judging recovery. Because 82% of these players had poor sleep, sleep is a practical area to review, although the study cannot show that improving sleep will change performance.
paper.athleteDev: Include a sleep questionnaire with resting heart rate, blood pressure and bleep-test VO2max when monitoring young players' readiness. Treat the link as an association: the study shows poorer sleep alongside weaker cardiovascular and fitness markers, not that sleep changes performance.
paper.rtp: The study used academy players and excluded anyone who dropped out because of injury or illness, so it does not address return to sport. It cannot be used to judge recovery from injury or readiness to return to training or competition.

records.sourceFile: The effect of acute sleep extension vs active recovery on post exercise recovery kinetics in rugby union players.pdf

paper.citation: Leduc C, Weaving D, Owen C, Ramirez-Lopez C, Chantler S, Aloulou A, et al. The effect of acute sleep extension vs active recovery on post exercise recovery kinetics in rugby union players. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(8):e0273026.
paper.abstract: Ten male university rugby union players completed a randomised single-blind crossover study comparing one night of sleep extension (time in bed up to 10 hours) with an early morning active recovery session after a late standardised training session. Physical, perceptual and cognitive recovery were measured before, immediately after, 14 h and 36 h after training.
paper.tldr: A single night of sleep extension after late training improved cognitive recovery at 14 h in university rugby players, but did not improve lower-body neuromuscular recovery, and made sleep more fragmented. Recovery status at 36 h did not differ between sleep extension and an early morning recovery session.
paper.methods: Randomised single-blind crossover over three weeks with 10 male university rugby players. Each week, players completed a standardised 19:30 full-contact session, then either extended sleep or attended a 07:30 active recovery session (15 min bike and 15 min mobility). Wristwatch actigraphy, a wellness questionnaire, a computerised Stroop test, heart rate recovery, running load index, countermovement jump and plyometric push-up were measured. Linear mixed models with effect sizes and magnitude-based decisions were used.
paper.findings: Sleep extension increased time in bed (very large vs control, first night) and total sleep time (most likely, first night; 07:00 vs 04:35, about 2 h 25 min more than control), but also produced greater sleep fragmentation than control (between-group effect 2.85 [2.00 to 3.70]). At 14 h, Stroop completion time was most likely shorter with sleep extension (between-group effect -1.53 [-2.33 to -0.74]), heart rate recovery was likely better with active recovery (-1.00 [-1.85 to -0.16]), and plyometric push-up flight time was likely longer with active recovery (-0.78 [-1.65 to 0.08], p > 0.05). Countermovement jump mean power was most likely to likely lower than baseline from 0 h to 36 h in both conditions. No between-group difference in recovery status was observed at 36 h.
paper.limitations: Twelve players were recruited but only 10 were analysed, and the study was in one squad. Actigraphy cannot measure sleep stages. Baseline sleep was below the recommended 7-9 hours, so a sleep debt may have masked effects. Chronotype was mid-range for all players and could not be analysed. There was no no-intervention control, so sleep extension was only compared with active recovery. The Discussion says HR recovery showed no substantial between-group difference, while the Results report a likely (p < 0.05) advantage for active recovery; the Results are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: When a late session is followed by a short turnaround, extending sleep may help cognitive recovery at 14 h, but it did not improve lower-body neuromuscular recovery. Staff should not expect a single night of sleep extension to speed overall recovery. The study also suggests an early morning active recovery session may not be needed for recovery status by 36 h.
paper.athleteDev: Sleep extension after late training may support cognitive readiness the next day, but it did not improve neuromuscular function and gave more fragmented sleep. Schedules that keep sleep timing consistent may be a safer option for performance staff to consider.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used to set return-to-play timing or clearance, since it measured healthy players after a standardised training session, not injury recovery.

records.sourceFile: The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Romdhani M, Souissi N, Dergaa I, Moussa-Chamari I, Chaabouni Y, Mahdouani K, et al. The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(4):1033-1042.
paper.abstract: Fourteen highly trained male judo athletes completed four randomised, double-blind sessions: placebo with no nap, a 20-minute nap with placebo, 5 mg/kg caffeine, and caffeine plus a 20-minute nap. Repeated sprint power, plasma energy and muscle-damage markers, and antioxidant enzymes were measured around a running-based anaerobic sprint test.
paper.tldr: A moderate caffeine dose (5 mg/kg) improved minimum sprint power and repeated sprint performance after a normal night's sleep, more than a 20-minute nap did. Caffeine also raised muscle-damage markers, while napping raised superoxide dismutase activity.
paper.methods: Randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover with 14 male international-level judo athletes, with sessions at least one week apart. Sessions were placebo, placebo with a 20-minute nap, caffeine (5 mg/kg), and caffeine with a nap, followed by the running-based anaerobic sprint test. Blood was sampled before and after exercise for lactate, glucose, creatine kinase, urea, AST, glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests and Cohen's d were used.
paper.findings: Compared with placebo, all treatments increased maximum and mean power on the sprint test (mean power rose by about 58 W with the nap, 90 W with caffeine and 128 W with caffeine plus nap, Table 2a). Minimum power was higher after caffeine and after caffeine plus nap than after placebo and than after the nap alone (versus nap: mean difference 58.6 W and 102 W). Post-exercise creatine kinase and urea were higher with caffeine, and AST was higher after caffeine plus nap than after the nap alone or caffeine alone. Superoxide dismutase rose versus placebo after the nap (p < 0.001) and after caffeine plus nap (p < 0.001), but not after caffeine alone. Glutathione peroxidase was not significant in the omnibus ANOVA or in any pairwise comparison against placebo in Table 2b. Plasma lactate rose only after the nap with placebo.
paper.limitations: The sample was 14 male judo athletes, all caffeine-naive, which limits generalisation. The sprint test is a laboratory protocol and not sport-specific. Sleep during the nap opportunity was only rated subjectively. No female athletes were tested. The authors say a sleep-deprived study with the same caffeine dose found no benefit, so the result may depend on prior sleep. The Results text says glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase rose only after napping, but Table 2b shows no significant glutathione peroxidase effect versus placebo; the table values were used here. The Discussion's explanations for the findings, such as aerobic glycolysis and sleep inertia, are not directly measured.
paper.practicalImplications: In rested, caffeine-naive athletes, a 5 mg/kg caffeine dose improved repeated sprint performance more than a 20-minute nap. A nap alone improved maximum and mean sprint power but not minimum power. Eleven of 14 participants had their highest minimum power in the caffeine-plus-nap session. Caffeine also raised post-exercise muscle-damage markers, so staff should weigh that cost.
paper.athleteDev: A 5 mg/kg caffeine dose before a repeated-sprint session can improve sprint power in rested, caffeine-naive athletes, and a short nap may add to this. Muscle-damage markers rose with caffeine, so the trade-off should be weighed. Results may not apply to habitual caffeine users.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy athletes in a laboratory sprint protocol and measured no injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes - Timing considerations.pdf

paper.citation: Arc-Chagnaud C, Dugué B, Bouzigon R, Pla R, Bosquet L, D-day Consortium, et al. The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024.
paper.abstract: The study aimed to test whether whole-body cryostimulation after training improves sleep and recovery, and which timing is best: immediately after training or one hour before bed. Twenty-two well-trained male athletes or triathletes completed three randomised crossover sessions. WBC did not change subjective or objective sleep, but it increased cardiac parasympathetic activity during deep sleep, most clearly after the exposure one hour before bed, where core body temperature was also lowest.
paper.tldr: In trained male endurance athletes, cryostimulation after evening training did not change any sleep measure, whether given straight after training or one hour before bed. The before-bed timing gave the clearest deep-sleep heart rate variability and core temperature changes.
paper.methods: Randomised controlled crossover protocol in 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes, run in winter with outdoor training at 5 to 10 C. Each completed a 70-minute interval running session at 18:00 and one night of home sleep analysis under WBC after training, WBC one hour before their own bedtime, or control, with sessions seven days apart; WBC was 30 s at -25 C then 3 min at -70 C. Sleep was measured with an EEG headband, wrist actigraphy, overnight heart rate variability, an ingested temperature pill and perceptual scales, analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: No sleep parameter differed between the three nights, including total sleep time, slow-wave sleep, sleep efficiency, movements and perceived sleep quality. Heart rate variability showed a condition effect only in the 10-minute slow-wave sleep window, with RMSSD, PNS index, SD1 and LF/HF favouring the 22:00 condition over control; whole-night and first-4-hour values did not differ. Core body temperature fell more after bedtime in the 22:00 condition, and muscle soreness and perceived recovery did not differ significantly between conditions.
paper.limitations: Only male participants were included, and the authors note that responses in women may differ and that the menstrual cycle was not considered. Each condition was measured over a single night in good sleepers during winter, which the authors say may not favour detecting sleep effects. The sample was small and well-trained, which limits extrapolation to other populations.
paper.practicalImplications: Cryostimulation after evening training did not change sleep in this group at either timing, so the data do not support using it as a sleep aid. If it is used for recovery, exposure about one hour before bed produced larger deep-sleep parasympathetic and core temperature changes than exposure straight after training.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff using whole-body cryostimulation with trained male endurance athletes, the study suggests a session about one hour before bed gives stronger overnight autonomic and temperature responses than one straight after an evening session. Whether these responses improve next-day performance was not tested.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy, well-trained athletes, and the study cannot show whether cryostimulation helps recovery after injury or during rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players - A parallel group-r.pdf

paper.citation: Altarriba-Bartes A, Vicens-Bordas J, Peña J, Alarcón-Palacios F, Sixtos-Meliton LA, Matabosch-Pijuan M, et al. The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players: A parallel group-randomized trial. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2023.
paper.abstract: The authors compared two comprehensive post-game recovery protocols in 18 players from the Mexican U-21 national team, randomised to a foam roller and tart cherry protocol or a stretching protocol, both with a carbohydrate-protein shake and cold-water immersion. Creatine kinase, jump, hamstring strength, perceived recovery and soreness were measured up to 68 h after a game. Both protocols showed time effects, and no significant differences were found between them.
paper.tldr: Two broad post-game recovery combinations gave similar creatine kinase, neuromuscular and soreness time courses in elite young players. Neither was shown to beat no intervention, because the trial had no control group.
paper.methods: Parallel-group randomised trial (registered NCT04716049) with block randomisation stratified by playing position. Players were allocated to protocol (a), a carbohydrate-protein shake, foam roller, 10 min cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice concentrate (n = 9), or protocol (b), a shake, static stretching and intermittent cold-water immersion (n = 9), after an unofficial game and the day after. Creatine kinase (CK-MM), countermovement jump, hamstring maximal voluntary contraction, perceived recovery and soreness were measured before, immediately after, and at 20, 44 and 68 h post-game and analysed with mixed models.
paper.findings: All outcomes showed large time effects, with no group main effect for any outcome. Creatine kinase peaked at 20 h and normalised by 68 h, while neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes returned to similar baseline levels by 44 h. Group by time interactions for countermovement jump, non-dominant hamstring strength and perceived recovery reflected changes only in protocol (a) at post-game and 20 h, including a 3.2 cm jump drop at 20 h versus 1.1 cm in protocol (b). The rise in creatine kinase from pre- to post-game correlated with accelerations, decelerations, high-speed running and sprint distance, but not total distance.
paper.limitations: Only male players were studied, the convenience sample was small, and there was no control group because the authors judged one unsuitable in this professional context. The abstract describes the interaction changes as being in 'neuromuscular and muscle soreness', but the results table shows the muscle soreness interaction was not significant (p = .34) and the significant perceptual interaction was for perceived recovery.
paper.practicalImplications: After a game, both recovery combinations in this trial produced similar time courses for creatine kinase, neuromuscular function and soreness, so the choice between them can rest on player preference and facilities. The trial cannot say whether either combination is better than standard care or rest.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study suggests the two recovery combinations are interchangeable for elite young male players over a 68 h post-game window. The link between creatine kinase rise and acceleration, deceleration and sprint loads is a single-game correlation in 18 players, not a validated tool for judging recovery.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The players were uninjured national-team members, and the study measured post-game recovery markers only, so it cannot guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The effects of cannabidiol oil on noninvasive measures of muscle damage in men.pdf

paper.citation: Cochrane-Snyman KC, Cruz C, Morales J, Coles M. The effects of cannabidiol oil on noninvasive measures of muscle damage in men. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2021;53(7):1460-1472.
paper.abstract: Investigated whether 150 mg CBD oil, compared with placebo, affects perceived soreness, arm circumference, joint angle, peak torque and RPE after eccentric elbow-flexor exercise in 13 untrained men. No condition effects or interactions were found, only time effects from the exercise-induced damage.
paper.tldr: A 150 mg daily CBD dose taken after eccentric arm exercise did not change soreness, arm swelling, joint angle or strength compared with placebo in untrained men. Soreness and joint angle changed over time in both conditions, showing the exercise caused some muscle damage.
paper.methods: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design in which 13 untrained men took 150 mg CBD (two 75 mg doses 8 h apart) or placebo on the exercise day and at 24 and 48 h, after 6 sets of 10 maximal eccentric elbow-flexor actions on an isokinetic dynamometer. Soreness, arm circumference, hanging joint angle, peak torque and RPE were measured before, after and at 24, 48 and 72 h.
paper.findings: No condition-by-time interaction or condition main effect was significant for perceived soreness, arm circumference, joint angle or peak torque (all P > 0.05). Time effects were significant for soreness (P < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.71), joint angle (P = 0.006) and RPE (P = 0.004). Peak torque fell about 12% from pre- to post-exercise across conditions, but this was not statistically significant across all visits.
paper.limitations: Only 13 untrained men were studied, with a single dose and schedule (about 2 mg/kg per day) and no blood markers of inflammation or muscle damage. The abstract describes four ANOVAs while the methods describe five (RPE included), and the age is given as 21 years in one place and 21.85 years in another.
paper.practicalImplications: For untrained adults, this dose and schedule of CBD oil would not be expected to reduce soreness or range-of-motion loss after heavy eccentric work, so the evidence does not support using it as a recovery aid at this dose.
paper.athleteDev: The study tested untrained men, so it does not apply directly to trained athletes. It gives no support for CBD as a performance-recovery aid at this dose.
paper.rtp: The study does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport and cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The effects of regular cold-water immersion use on training-induced changes in strength and endurance performance - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Malta ES, Dutra YM, Broatch JR, Bishop DJ, Zagatto AM. The Effects of Regular Cold-Water Immersion Use on Training-Induced Changes in Strength and Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Meta-analysis of 8 controlled studies of regular post-training cold-water immersion (CWI) during resistance or endurance training. CWI was associated with smaller strength gains, but did not change endurance performance gains.
paper.tldr: Regular cold-water immersion after resistance training appears to blunt strength gains. After endurance training it did not change aerobic performance gains in these studies.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of MEDLINE, CENTRAL and SPORTDiscus searched to 25 November 2019, registered on PROSPERO (CRD42018098898). Included controlled trials with CWI at 15 C or below after training of at least 3 weeks, with baseline and post-training strength or aerobic performance measures; quality was rated with the PEDro scale and risk of bias with the Cochrane tool, and effects were pooled as standardised mean differences.
paper.findings: In resistance training, CWI reduced gains in 1RM, maximal isometric strength and strength endurance (overall SMD -0.60, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.33; p < 0.0001) and in ballistic efforts (overall SMD -0.61, 95% CI -1.11 to -0.11; p = 0.02). In endurance training, CWI had no effect on time-trial mean power or maximal aerobic power (overall SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.53; p = 0.71) or on time-trial duration (overall SMD 0.00; p = 1.00).
paper.limitations: Eight studies with 470 volunteers, mean PEDro quality 5.3 (moderate), no studies blinded, and most with unclear or high risk of bias for randomisation. Water temperature and duration varied widely across studies, and the endurance and resistance subgroups were small (4 to 5 studies each). Participants were trained, physically active, recreationally active or sedentary men rather than competitive athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest avoiding regular cold-water immersion during training blocks focused on strength, hypertrophy or power, and say it may be most useful around competition when heavy resistance training is not typical. They note the optimal temperature and duration for training adaptation is unknown.
paper.athleteDev: For strength, hypertrophy or power blocks, avoid scheduling regular post-session cold-water immersion. For endurance blocks, regular immersion did not change aerobic gains in these studies, so the decision should rest on recovery needs rather than expected adaptation.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: all participants were healthy and the outcomes were training adaptations, not injury recovery, rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: The effects of relaxation techniques following acute, high intensity football training on parasympathetic reactivation.pdf

paper.citation: Renaghan E, Wishon MJ, Wittels HL, Feigenbaum LA, Bellamy K, Hatfield M, et al. The effects of relaxation techniques following acute, high intensity football training on parasympathetic reactivation. Front Sports Act Living. 2023;5:1267631.
paper.abstract: Thirty-eight Division-I male football players were measured under three post-training conditions: 15 minutes of guided mindfulness, 15 minutes of rest, or no intervention. Both relaxation conditions produced larger drops in heart rate and respiration rate and larger HRV increases than no intervention.
paper.tldr: A 15-minute guided mindfulness session or a seated rest period after high-intensity football training lowered heart rate and breathing rate and raised HRV more than usual post-training activity. Staff could use either as a low-equipment step, but the effect was measured in one squad over single sessions.
paper.methods: Repeated-measures, non-randomised design with each athlete tested in all three conditions, one Monday per condition, after routine preseason training. Heart rate, respiration rate, SDNN and rMSSD were recorded with an armband monitor (Warfighter Monitor) before, during and after the 15-minute intervention and analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey correction.
paper.findings: Heart rate fell by 81.6 bpm after mindfulness, 66.4 bpm after rest and 40.9 bpm after no intervention, and both relaxation conditions produced larger falls than no intervention (p < 0.0000), with mindfulness larger than rest (p < 0.05). Post-intervention SDNN was 46.9 ms after mindfulness, 42.9 ms after rest and 33.1 ms after no intervention, and rMSSD was 17.9, 16.7 and 13.8 ms respectively.
paper.limitations: Condition order was fixed by week, so condition and time cannot be separated, and the design is not randomised. Group sizes (35, 36, 33) do not match the stated sample of 38, no a priori power analysis was run, and four authors are employees of Tiger Tech Solutions, which owns the Warfighter Monitor. SDNN and rMSSD labels are inconsistent between the results text, Table 1 and Table 2, so the HRV values should be read with caution.
paper.practicalImplications: A 15-minute guided mindfulness session or seated rest straight after a high-intensity session is a low-equipment way to lower heart rate and raise HRV in the short term. Mindfulness produced larger falls in heart rate and breathing rate than rest, but that comparison is also confounded by the fixed week order.
paper.athleteDev: A 15-minute block of guided breathing or seated rest in the minutes after hard training can bring heart rate down faster than usual post-training activity. The study did not measure performance or next-day readiness, so it does not show that this improves either.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: it tested starters after single training sessions, with no injured or returning players and no readiness or performance outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The effects of travel on performance a - 13 year analysis of the National Rugby League NRL competition.pdf

paper.citation: Read DB, Williams S, Fullagar HHK, Weakley JJS. The effects of travel on performance: a 13-year analysis of the National Rugby League (NRL) competition. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022;6(1):60-65.
paper.abstract: Analysis of 2,352 NRL matches (2007 to 2019) found that longer away travel was associated with a lower chance of winning and a smaller points difference. The effect of travel shrank over the 13 seasons, with no clear differences between states.
paper.tldr: In the NRL, each 1,000 km of away travel was linked to a small drop in winning chances and in points margin. The effect has shrunk over time, but the win-probability estimate is imprecise.
paper.methods: Exploratory retrospective analysis of official NRL match results from 2007 to 2019, excluding draws, play-offs and matches where a team played a home fixture outside its home city. Win or loss was modelled with a generalised linear mixed model and points difference with a linear mixed model, with team nested within season as a random effect and covariates for away disadvantage, turnaround time and opposition final ranking; travel was the straight-line distance from the away team's home stadium to the venue.
paper.findings: Each 1,000 km of travel was associated with a 2.7% lower win probability (95% CI -5.7 to 0.3%) and a 1.1-point lower points difference (95% CI -2.0 to -0.2). Playing away had an odds ratio of 0.56 (0.48 to 0.66) for winning, and the travel effect was largest in 2007 to 2009 (-2.7%, 95% CI -4.7 to -0.6%) and close to zero in 2018 to 2019 (1.1%, 95% CI -1.2 to 3.3%).
paper.limitations: Not all travel-related factors could be measured, travel outside matches was unknown, and no individual athlete measures were collected. The team's own ability was not modelled, and the single Victorian team (six titles in 13 seasons) showed no travel penalty, so the authors say a team-by-team analysis is needed.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can estimate the likely effect of an away trip on match outcome and use it when planning travel logistics, sleeping arrangements and nutrition. The authors note that teams travelling more than 2,000 km for away matches could expect about 2.2 fewer points and a 5.4% lower winning likelihood on average.
paper.athleteDev: Use the travel distance of an away fixture as a planning input for sleep, meals and logistics, because longer trips were linked to small average performance losses in this league. The study does not show that any specific travel strategy reduces those losses.
paper.rtp: Does not inform return to sport: it analyses team match results for players in the competition, with no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play data.

records.sourceFile: The impact of daytime napping following normal night time sleep on physical performance - A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression.pdf

paper.citation: Boukhris O, Trabelsi K, Suppiah H, Ammar A, Clark CCT, Jahrami H, et al. The Impact of Daytime Napping Following Normal Night-Time Sleep on Physical Performance: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Meta-regression. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies (269 physically active or athletic participants) comparing daytime naps with no nap after normal night sleep. Naps improved 5-m shuttle run highest distance, total distance and fatigue index, with no clear effect on muscle force.
paper.tldr: A nap after a normal night's sleep improved 5-m shuttle run distance and reduced fatigue in these studies. The evidence for sprint, jump, Wingate, repeated sprint and endurance outcomes is too thin to recommend napping for those measures.
paper.methods: A PRISMA-guided search of seven databases, supplemented by reference lists and expert contact, with QualSyst quality ratings. Random-effects meta-analysis, heterogeneity statistics, sensitivity and cumulative analyses, publication bias tests and meta-regression were used, and only physically active or athletic participants with normal night sleep were included.
paper.findings: Compared with no nap, napping increased 5-m shuttle run highest distance (ES 1.026, 95% CI 0.718 to 1.334) and total distance (ES 0.737, 95% CI 0.488 to 0.985), and reduced fatigue index (ES 0.839, 95% CI 0.211 to 1.458). Muscle force did not change (ES 0.175, p=0.267). Meta-regression suggested a longer gap between the end of the nap and exercise was associated with a larger fatigue index reduction (p=0.04).
paper.limitations: Most studies estimated nap duration or used actigraphy, so sleep stages and sleep inertia were not measured. Participants were almost all male, and studies after sleep restriction or deprivation were excluded, so the findings do not cover those conditions.
paper.practicalImplications: After a normal night's sleep, a daytime nap before an afternoon session may help repeated shuttle-sprint performance like the 5-m shuttle run test. A longer gap between the end of the nap and exercise was linked to a larger fatigue index benefit, so allow time to clear sleep inertia; nap duration itself did not moderate the effect.
paper.athleteDev: For repeated shuttle-sprint work after a normal night's sleep, a nap with enough time to wake fully before training may help. Benefits for sprint, jump, strength and endurance performance are not established.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return to sport, because it included physically active people and athletes after normal sleep and no injured or recovering athletes.
